sources: The Scientist, The Earwig's Tale (May Berenbaum, entomologist, University of Illinois): surveying about ten centuries of literature she could find only a single report of an earwig in an ear; https://www.the-scientist.com/the-earwigs-tale-43480

University of California IPM, Earwigs (Pest Notes): not harmful to people, though they can pinch if trapped in clothing or sat on; feed at night on aphids, insect eggs and plant shoots, can damage seedlings; hide by day in dark, cool, moist places; come indoors when outdoor conditions are too dry, hot or cold; pincers somewhat curved in males, straighter in females; most species have wings under short hard covers but seldom fly; females dig cells in soil, lay masses of 30 or more eggs, and nymphs are protected and fed by their mother until their first molt; rolled newspaper or tubes placed on soil before dark collect earwigs, emptied each morning; https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/earwigs/

Science News, Earwigs take origami to extremes to fold their wings (2018, on Faber, Arrieta and Studart, Science): earwigs pack their wings into packages with a surface area more than 10 times smaller than unfurled; ETH Zurich team built folding structures inspired by them for possible use in robotics, biomedical devices and spacecraft; https://www.sciencenews.org/article/earwigs-take-origami-extremes-fold-their-wings

beats.say: Number ten. The earwig. Pincers on its rear end, and named after your ear.
The myth says it crawls into your ear while you sleep.
One entomologist searched ten centuries of writing, and found one single case.
Those pincers can give you a pinch, if one gets trapped in your clothes.
It wanders indoors when it's too dry outside. At night, it hunts aphids and insect eggs.
Earwig. D tier. A pinch at worst. And your ears are safe. Myth busted.
